A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Formal model.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.
Problem 97. Majority rule and a protected right: case 2
Knowledge context.
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.
Given facts.

A council of 20 members votes 14 to 6 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to use the public library equally. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
Rules.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Task.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Vote check: 14>6, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (use the public library equally) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
Answer.
It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.
Knowledge takeaway.
A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Formal model.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.
